Public Health Law is a course that examines the foundations and complexity of law, policy, and public health practice in the United States. Exploration includes constitutional foundations of public health, regulatory frameworks, the judiciary, and legal tools available to protect and promote population health. Contemporary challenges in public health are prioritized in course work and will include, but not be limited to emergency preparedness, populations health outcomes as a result of legal systems, and the balance of individuals rights and collective good. This course is designed for medical students, and graduate and doctoral students in public health, public administration, public policy, and healthcare administration. The course emphasizes practical application of legal principles to real-world policy and law frameworks.

Statistical methods for time-to-event data. Some statistical theory is covered for the benefit of master of statistics students, but mostly this is an applied course accessible to non-statisticians using the Stata statistical software.  No previous experience with Stata is required. Topics include: life tables, survival estimates (e.g., Kaplan-Meier), survival distributions, non-regression survival tests (e.g., logrank test), Cox proportional hazards model, recurrent event Cox models, clustered data shared frailty Cox models, parametric time-to-event models, competing risk models, time-varying covariates, power and sample size for survival analysis.

Assessing community needs, being able to identify strengths and weaknesses, and working collaboratively with stakeholders are important skills for any public health professional. This course familiarizes students with concepts and approaches for community health assessment and analysis. The course will include strategies, methods and measures for assessing the health of a community. Special focus will be placed on the application of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods as well as Community Based Participatory approaches.

Basic principles of epidemiology, including fundamentals of epidemiologic study design and data resources with emphasis on determining causation of chronic disease. Students will learn to explain the role of quantitative and qualitative methods in describing and assessing a population’s health, as well as the importance of evidence-based practice in the field of public health.

Basic principles of epidemiology, including fundamentals of epidemiologic study design and data resources with emphasis on determining causation of chronic disease. Students will learn to explain the role of quantitative and qualitative methods in describing and assessing a population’s health, as well as the importance of evidence-based practice in the field of public health.

This course is designed to teach you the rudiments of effective research.  This course will combine lecture, seminar, and hands-on approaches.  You will be responsible for choosing a topic for your thesis or dissertation, or some other research, and creating a proposal. You will also be responsible for obtaining and providing reviewer comments (i.e. student/peer comments) at different points throughout the semester.  You will learn methods of public health and clinical investigation.  You will gain experience in identifying a research topic, preparing a research proposal, and presenting and defending a research plan.  You will also gain experience in acting as a research collaborator and reviewer.
Course is designed to provide an overview of the foundations and epidemiologic methods used in assessing the phenomena of infectious disease from a public health perspective.

Provides students with the opportunity to apply principles of leadership, governance, and management while applying negotiation and mediation skills to address organizational or community challenges in a public health setting. Students will learn basic principles and tools for budget and resource management, discuss multiple dimensions of the policy-making process, and propose strategies to identify stakeholders and build partnerships to influence public health outcomes. An emphasis will be placed on the importance of advocacy for political, social, or economic policies and programs that will improve health in diverse populations.

An introduction to the field of public health, including history, philosophy, values, core functions and the ten essential services. A comparison of the organization, structure, and function of health care, public health, and regulatory systems, both nationally and internationally, with emphasis on the effects of globalization and the burden of disease. Students will discuss the policy-making process, population needs, the science of prevention in population health, and major causes/trends of morbidity and mortality in relevant communities. Emphasis on the importance of evidence-based practice in the field of public health. Public health professionals from local and state health departments, non-profit organizations, and academia provide varied insights on public health programs and careers.

This course provides a comprehensive examination of the global health ecosystem and the distribution of disease burden across low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Through critical analysis of global health data and information systems, students develop skills in comparative health systems analysis, examining epidemiological trends and health outcomes within and between countries. Students design evidence-based intervention strategies and apply monitoring and evaluation techniques for global health programs and policies.

This course will consider disease and illness within socio-cultural contexts. Emphasis will be placed on the ethical, behavioral, psychological, social, cultural, political and economic factors that influence the prevention/treatment of medical and public health problems and theories of health behavior that inform public health practice. The student will develop abilities to assess population needs that affect communities’ health, form effective communication strategies and develop important cultural competence in communicating public health content. Furthermore, students will be able to demonstrate the means by which structural bias, social inequalities and racism undermine health equity at organizational, community and social levels.

This Graduate-level course prepares students to develop a public health disaster preparedness and response plan for their jurisdiction. The course combines traditional community health program planning with disaster management in order to develop effective programs for preparing communities to respond to disasters.

This course will address special topics in public health which are of value as electives for public health students, but which can not be taught regularly. Multiple sections might be taught in a single semester, addressing different topics. Students would be permitted to repeat the course for degree credit for a new topic.

The course will provide graduate students with theory and application of Statistical Learning methods for data analysis. Statistical Learning refers to a set of techniques for understanding complex and messy datasets. In addition to simple and multivariable linear regression topics, techniques for supervised and unsupervised learning, data reduction, and classification will be introduced and strategies for evaluating estimate precision and estimation of classifier accuracy and model validity will be provided. The focus of the class will be applied with emphasis on using and understanding the results of statistical software in a Public Health context.

A continuation of Epidemiology I (FP MD 6300). Intermediate and advanced principles in epidemiology, with emphasis on study designs, selection/information biases, confounding and effect modification.  Students will learn how to plan an epidemiologic study, analyze data from epidemiologic studies, critique the epidemiologic literature and prepare epidemiologic reports.

This course will cover primary data collection techniques relevant to epidemiological and public health research, including survey methodology, instrument design and testing, direct observation, key informant interviews and focus groups, qualitative methodology, and SEIR (susceptible-infectious-exposed-removed) models. Students will learn, through hands-on projects, how to develop primary data collection tools, as well as analysis and interpretation of associated data. The course builds on concepts and techniques presented in Epidemiology II (PBHLT 7300) and Biostatistics II (PBHLT 7100 or PHS 7000).

This course examines legal and policy foundations of public health practice in Utah and the U.S. exploring how federal, state, and local governments develop and implement policies that protect population health. The course also provides a comprehensive overview of federal, state, and local governments’ roles in developing and implementing health policies, including public health authority, legal frameworks, public health emergencies, global public health, administrative law, environmental health, marginalization, social determinants of health, and ethics. Students are presented with strategies and skills for effective health leadership, including detailed research on critical health policy. Students develop practical skills in policy analysis, stakeholder engagement, and evidence-based advocacy, culminating in a comprehensive policy evaluation that demonstrates their ability to assess and influence policies for improved health outcomes across diverse populations.

This course will cover theoretical concepts for effective adult learning, skills for classroom management, active learning, syllabus preparation, and objective-based evaluation. Students will have the opportunity to develop class plans, develop and deliver and review recorded lectures, prepare and use evaluation tools, and receive feedback from peers and faculty.
A series of seminars from faculty and staff from within and outside of the Public Health Program on a variety of topics pertaining to public health.

A series of seminars from faculty and staff from within and outside of the Public Health Program on a variety of topics pertaining to public health. The course is meant for entering doctoral students, as well as MSPH students.The human health seminar (1 credit of the total 3 credit seminar series) focuses on foundational knowledge competencies related to human health. Topic areas include: effects of environmental, biological, genetic, behavioral, psychological factors on population health; social, political, and economic determinants of health; globalization; and One Health.

In this course, students will write a narrative literature review that summarizes the available knowledge on a topic, synthesizes multiple points of view and approaches, and identifies where and how new research may advance our current understanding. The semester will follow the process of writing a review from conceptualization to completion: we will first establish a research question and the aims of the review before planning and iteratively refining a search of two peer-reviewed databases, screening sources for relevance, creating a literature matrix, and finally drafting and revising the review.

This course investigates the modern history of environmental politics and explores a range of policy regimes including climate change, air quality, chemicals and toxics, natural resource, energy systems, nuclear energy, and energy politics. We explore lessons about success and failure and consider the innovation needed to ensure durable policy making in each area. Each issue area illustrates the opportunities and obstacles that regimes face in the process of environmental politics. Arguments focusing on population, economic development, income inequality, and sustainability will also be discussed and analyzed. We consider a range of perspectives and notions of valuing the environmental goods around us. Ultimately, the goal is to create a toolbox of perspectives to help key stakeholders, like yourself, evaluate, design, legislate, and implement key policy programs associated with complex environmental issues.

This course is a study of how privileges, opportunities, and rights and are distributed within society and how such distribution is (and can be) shaped by human agency and sociopolitical institutions. Course materials combine historical and contemporary empirical analysis to help analyze the extent to which and how societal disparities are grounded in and perpetuated by government policies, cultural traditions, and social customs. Course activities and assignments examine and articulate how the social (in)justice is reflected in their relevant political, cultural, and social contexts, as well as their individual personal, professional, and civic experiences.

Introduction To Occupational Therapy

This course offers in-depth exploration of occupation, the primary modality of occupational therapy. Emphasis will be on appreciation of occupation in personal experience in order to be more effective in therapeutic applications of occupation. Topics include: occupations in history, personal meaning of occupations, pleasure/play and leisure, productivity/paid and unpaid work, restoration/sleep and waking rest, temporal dimensions of occupation, spatial patterns in occupations, sociocultural context of occupation, and effective therapeutic use of occupations in practice.

This foundational course offers a comprehensive overview of occupational therapy (OT) practice through the lens of time, exploring the evolution of OT as a health profession. Students will learn about the core concept of occupation, occupational science, and occupation-based theories that underpin OT practice. Key topics include occupational engagement, participation, and health, as well as professional values, ethics, standards of practice, and continuing competence. The course culminates in the creation of a professional development plan that students will refine throughout their program.

This course explicitly highlights self-awareness and interpersonal communication as integral to therapeutic relating, professional development, working with other professionals, and to therapeutically relate to clients, students, families, and populations with various cultural differences. Learners will have the opportunity to identify strengths and areas for professional development in interactive communication skills during class using the intentional relationship model. Students will examine how culture affects them as practitioners of occupational therapy as well as how culture shapes the occupations and perceived needs of their clients. By having a deeper appreciation of the ubiquitous role of culture in the therapeutic relationship, students will deepen their understanding of factors that can affect how therapy is perceived by clients. Building on this understanding, students will further examine therapeutic use of self and begin to develop interviewing skills necessary to build rapport and to collaborate with clients. This course will also demonstrate how ethical reasoning needs to be employed when relating to clients of all backgrounds. To enhance understanding of the clients’ occupational needs occupational justice and emerging practice areas will be highlighted.

This course uses historical and contemporary perspective of human occupation and the meaning occupation provides for human function. Focusing on engagement in activity, students will be given the opportunity to develop their skills in selected media, examine the role of creative process, develop their skills in task analysis and develop a foundation for clinical reasoning.

This course develops a functional knowledge of human anatomy and movement, as they relate to occupation. The study of normal human motion is crucial to recognizing and determining deviations in movement as a result of varying health problems. Furthermore, this course develops knowledge and understanding of the nervous, muscular, skeletal, and cardiovascular systems as they relate to normal human anatomy and pathological conditions. This course includes a human body dissection lab.

This course is designed to give students background knowledge and skills related to the OT process as a preparation for subsequent coursework in adults, pediatric, and mental health practice areas. Students will understand the OT domain and threshold concepts including occupations, client factors, performance skills, performance skills, performance patterns, and context and environment. Students will also begin to develop skills needed in the OT process such as interview skills, observation skills, clinical reasoning skills, and documentation skills. These skills will be foundational for subsequent courses.

Students deepen their understanding of the occupational therapy process in pediatrics by addressing complex occupational performance problems in childhood and adolescence. The course advances professional reasoning through the selection and application of conceptual models, assessments, and evidence-based interventions with a variety of pediatric clients. Emphasis is placed on clinical decision-making, reimbursement considerations, and documentation practices that communicate the value of occupational therapy across settings. Students will apply the occupational therapy process with a community client and during supervised pediatric fieldwork, developing skills needed to demonstrate entry-level competence in pediatric occupational therapy.

This is the third course in the OT Process – Adults series.  It is structured under the organizing practice model of PEO and incorporates the Biomechanical/Rehabilitative models to frame assessment, treatment, and evidence-based practice for clients with orthopedic conditions. Students will learn to select appropriate outcome measures, plan and implement treatment, and evaluate evidence related to best practices for clients. Interventions will include splinting and thermal modalities, ADL adaptations, and home exercise programs. Clinical reasoning, occupation-based practice, and client-centered care will be taught and threaded through course activities and assignments.

The rationale and process for developing occupation-based programs either in the community or reaching out to the community at the population level will be explored in-depth. Using community-engaged learning principles, students will identify, explore, & complete a needs assessment, & develop a community-based, occupation-centered program with a program evaluation component. Factors considered will be service delivery models, social & occupational justice perspectives, family & caregiver dynamics, health promotion, professional communication & leadership skills, and current evidence relevant to the population and context of each new program developed by the students. The Level 1 FW experience will be completed in a rural area or with an urban agency assisting an under-served population.

This is the second of two courses required in the research sequence. Building on their knowledge and experiences from the first research course, students will further their knowledge of quantitative and qualitative research practice by creating research proposals and a grant proposal. This course will focus on the development of teaching and learning skills applicable across a variety of settings.  Principles of adult learning theory will be explored in detail as they relate to academic and clinical education.  Students will learn the process of instructional design including developing course objectives, assessment instruments an grading criteria.  Students will develop teaching skills appropriate for varying audiences (student, peers, clients) and the type of setting (academic, clinical, and professional conferences/workshops).  Mechanisms to enhance both presentations and delivery of material will be emphasized, along with learning different formats using advanced technology.  Opportunities to receive and provide feedback to others will be provided.

Students practice evaluation, treatment, and documentation procedures under the supervision of a licensed occupational therapist. This course is credit hours for the semester.

This course series will serve as the context for preparing students for their 14-week capstone experience that occurs at the end of this program. The goal of the capstone experience includes designing an individual plan to develop advanced skills in one of the following areas: clinical practice skills, research skills, leadership, program and policy development, or education. The second aim is to participate in community-engaged learning by developing objectives that are responsive to the capstone site’s needs. In this first course of the capstone series, students will formulate ideas for their capstone project/experience topic. Following their ideas, students will complete a literature review on their topic of interest. After considering professional and project goals, students will narrow down sites that can meet their objectives and start connecting with community sites to determine a potential capstone location. By the end of the semester, students will begin to a) develop a relationship with an experiential site mentor to explore population-based needs at a site and b) write their proposal for their potential capstone project/experience.

The third capstone course will allow students, with advisor guidance, to revisit, refine, and revise their capstone project before the experiential component and final report. This will include additional searches of the literature, the completion of a second needs assessment, the creation of an activity outline for their capstone project, and the development of a program evaluation assessment. This will allow the capstone students to maintain communication with their sites before arriving during their final semester of the OTD curriculum.

This course outlines the theory and employment of weapons systems. Students explore the processes of detection, evaluation, threat analysis, weapon selection, delivery, guidance, and explosives. Students are required to participate in a three hour lab each week which gives hands on training for the above and a one hour physical fitness course, three times a week.

A concentrated physical- and military-skills training program to prepare students for participation in a regional military skills competition. Intense physical training requirements and rigorous training schedule. Focus on teamwork and physical, mental, and emotional endurance. Students must be enrolled in MIL S 1010, 1020, 2010, 2020, 3010, 3020, 4010, or 4020 in order to participate.

A concentrated course of study that combines key elements of the Military Science 1000- and 2000-level courses. The purpose of this class is to qualify students for the Army ROTC Advance Camp. For students who have missed one semester of 1000- or 2000-level courses.

Development of leadership skills within the framework of Army small-unit tactics and leadership. Course includes instruction on techniques for setting goals and standards, motivating and utilizing subordinates, coping with disruptive influences, and developing physical stamina. Instructor assesses student's leadership potential and establishes a program to strengthen deficient leadership dimensions. Realistic simulation exercises in leadership, decision-making, planning, organizing, delegation, administrative control, and interpersonal skills. Assessed proficiency in these areas provides an effective forecast of leadership effectiveness.
Students select advanced topics of interest and arrange credit under program adviser supervision in areas related to military science.

This course focuses on situational dynamics during times of conflict.  It will introduce students to the dynamic challenges that leaders find themselves while serving in the Military.  As part of a team, all students will take on the mantle of key players of America's Military History.

Analysis of training management and other staff procedures as they relate to contemporary military leadership. Study of the military justice system and its application. A study of various ethical and professional issues related to junior military officers. Selected topics in advanced leadership and officership designed to prepare the student for commissioning as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army.
For students who wish to explore a professional military subject prior to commissioning. Topics and credit are arranged with program adviser.

This course explores how physical science principles govern modern resource extraction and materials flow. Students will unearth not only how mining really works, but also how it affects their daily life, from ore bodies to everyday devices. Minecraft Java Edition will be used as both a collaborative space and a sandbox laboratory for intellectual edification. Students will design and test mining systems, analyze energy/throughput/pollution trade-offs, evaluate scientific claims and sources, and propose mitigation and reclamation strategies. Through international mining case studies and class discussions, students will practice civil discourse, compare worldviews, and examine how social, economic, and environmental systems interconnect and influence their lives. No prior video gaming or mining experience required.

This course introduces two basic skills important for engineers, graphics-centric computational design using Vulcan, and Python programming. In Python, students will be introduced to basic programming concepts including variables, expressions, conditional statements, iteration, and lists.

Introduction to mineral resources, extraction methods and plant practices. Basic principles and operations of extractive metallurgy. Historical perspective of processing of metallic materials.

Introduction to metallurgical processing fundamentals and applied technology that are to separate minerals and chemically process minerals to produce high purity metals as well as the application of these principles and technologies in areas such as biomedical devices and sensors, energy conversion and storage, and nuclear material processing.

Continuation of Metallurgical thermodynamics I in which changes in Gibb’s free energy and chemical potential are used to work with phase and chemical reaction equilibrium problems. Covers single phase equilibrium, multi-component phase equilibrium, non-ideal gas equations of state, ideal and non-ideal solutions, chemical reactions involving gaseous and condensed phases, construction and interpretation of phase diagrams, electrochemistry, and equilibrium behavior of ionic solutions.

This course will allow students to earn academic credit for the successful completion of a Materials Science and Engineering-related internship in a research lab. To have an internship fulfill a Technical Elective requirement, students must earn a total of 3 credit hours and complete research assignments as encouraged by the faculty mentor. The internship progress will be monitored, evaluated, and graded by the research faculty mentor. Students must take an active role in finding and applying for an appropriate internship before enrolling for the course.

This course is designed to teach students about engineering and applications of materials in the biomedical applications with an emphasis on devices and sensors. Students will gain an understanding of the entire life cycle of materials starting form the extraction of materials to engineering devices, to end-of-life disposal. Students will gain hands on experience in device fabrications methods and will be required to build and demonstrate a biomedical device as part of the course. Students will use Arduino boards and python for sensor instrumentation and data acquisition. At the end of the course, students will understand how to design a biomedical device/sensor with the appropriate materials and fabrication methods.

Phase transformations in metals and alloys: Elementary physical chemistry of phases, phase diagrams and phase rule application, diffusion in solids, structure of interfaces, nucleation and growth, solidification, pearlitic, bainitic, massive and order-disorder transformations, precipitation, elementary treatment of martensitic transformation, iron-carbon system, and heat-treatment of steels. Laboratory sessions illustrate principles developed in lectures.

Powder preparation, rapid-solidification processing principles, powder characterization, theory of compaction, sintering, full-density processing, powder metallurgy component design, compact characterization, application of powder metallurgy processing to structural, electrical, magnetic, and biomedical components. The laboratory sessions are a integral part of the course. Participation by students is mandatory. The credit hour for the laboratory portion is 1.0. Laboratory schedule and location will be determined during the semester.

This class covers concepts in renewable energy including, solar thermal, wind, photovoltaics, fuel cells, geothermal, and biofuels. Students will have an opportunity for hands-on experience with these energy technologies through labs conducted through the Roger and Dawn Crus Renewable Energy Center.

This course introduces the design, performance, and application of advanced materials in aerospace systems, with a special focus on manufacturing in zero-gravity and space environments. Topics include metals, ceramics, and composites for extreme aerospace conditions; the physics of materials processing in microgravity; additive and cold spray manufacturing in orbit; and in-situ resource utilization of lunar and Martian regolith. Case studies from NASA, DoD, and commercial space companies highlight real-world applications. Students complete a team project designing a material or manufacturing solution for a space environment.

Stress and strain analysis, Mohr's circle, yield criteria, elastic and plastic deformation, deformation of single and polycrystals, dislocations, strengthening mechanisms, fatigue, creep and fracture of metals. Also involves a design problem of material selection for gas-turbine blades on the basis of mechanical property requirements.

The course focuses on fundamentals of steel making, including hot iron pretreatment, refining (both converter and electric arc furnace), continuous casting, and hot rolling. Flowsheet and process parameters for selected steel products will be discussed in class. Hands-on experiences include metallographic analysis of steel samples and a field trip to the Nucor Plymouth plant in northern Utah.

Advanced statistical methods applied to solve engineering problems and to analyze massive experimental database. One-factor experiments, simple, and multiple linear regression, statistical quality control and response surface method.

This course provides the student with a brief applied understanding of societal ethics, engineering ethics and personal morals. Steps and procedures in ethical decision making are presented. Famous engineering ethical cases are analyzed to identify common reasons individuals behaved unethically. Tools for how to protect oneself in ethical situations are discussed. Some principles of engineering professionalism are also covered.

This lab facilitates hands-on experience with manufacturing practices for the purpose of informing an understanding of design principles, and to supplement material covered in the ME EN 2650 Manufacturing of Engineering Systems lecture class. The lab will emphasize understanding of dimensional units and tolerances as they relate to manufacturability, economy, and performance. Students will interpret and modify drawing sets, and consider the elements of effective communication with the manufacturing environment. Safe lab practices and use of machinery and tools will be introduced and practiced. Basic principles of material removal (machining) will be discussed and demonstrated, and compared with modern approaches (CNC and beyond). Cutting tool materials will be presented and compared, with an emphasis on productive manufacturing approaches and tool economy. The importance of standards for communicating design intent will be emphasized. By the end of the course, the student will obtain: i) experience interfacing with the manufacturing resources which exist within the Department and on campus, ii) opportunities to specify, measure, and revise tolerances and evaluate the effect of tolerances on assemblies (interference, MMC, etc.), iii) experience using real, durable, commonly available engineering materials in design and assemblies.

This course focuses on the modeling, analysis and control of dynamic systems. The modeling portion of the course includes mechanical, electrical, electromechanical, thermal, and fluidic systems. Methods employed involve solving sets of coupled differential equations using time-domain (i.e., state-space), frequency-domain (i.e., Laplace transform), and numerical techniques. The control-systems portion of the course focuses on the use frequency-domain techniques, and includes topics such as block diagrams, stability analysis, steady-state error, PID control, and root-locus design.

Model and simulate the dynamics of advanced mechatronic systems consisting of a variety of energy domains (mechanical, electrical, magnetic, hydraulic, thermofluidic). Students will learn to use Bond Graph techniques and state space formulation for linear and nonlinear systems. Hands- on recitation exercises in class allow students to practice modeling techniques on a variety of mechatronic devices. For a final project, students will model and simulate a complex dynamic system.

Case-based sessions covering clinical trails in occlusive heart disease, arthritis, asthma, kidney disease and oncology provide informative examples of trail design and potential pitfalls.

The course considers in some depth the epidemiologic study designs: cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, ecological.  Goals are that students will be able to: 1) design epidemiologic studies; 2) understand causal inference and potential sources of bias in observational studies; 3) recognize and address confounding and effect modification in data; and 4) critically read epidemiologic papers.

This project-based course is designed to give students experience designing and conducting cost-effectiveness analyses using either Excel or TreeAge Pro. Students will be expected to perform all components necessary to complete a cost-effectiveness analysis and be prepared to write up a manuscript based on the analysis performed.

Personalized Health Care is the tailoring of medical treatment to the individual characteristics of each patient. This course will review the fundamental elements of Personalized Health Care, discuss relevant case studies of preventive and therapeutic applications of Personalized Health Care, and explore future developments. Students will also have the opportunity to devise ways in which Personalized Health Care can be advanced locally, nationally, and globally.

Clinical Problem Solving for Medical Technology Innovations introduces students to a structured method for developing high-impact, innovative, disruptive medical devices and technologies with potential for successful commercialization and translation into real-world clinical practice. The foundation of this method is the structure described in the Stanford Biodesign system (Yack et al., see textbook information below). Students will learn to approach real-world clinical problems from a multidisciplinary global perspective, and then to identify diagnostic and therapeutic deficiencies that can be addressed through the process of innovating medical technologies. Students will also learn to incorporate end-user feedback, U.S. FDA regulatory assessment, intellectual property (IP) assessment, and business commercialization perspectives in the initial development of new technologies. This course will provide the academic foundation for mastery of a structured medical technology innovation and development process from clinical needs finding to needs analysis. Online module completion, textbook chapter reading assignments, and self-study assignments are critical.

The seminars are designed to illustrate the process of scientific discovery in clinical investigation providing examples of how innovative approaches and methods were applied and to discuss obstacles that impede progress.

This course explores the interplay between pharmaceutical economics and policy in the US, emphasizing the historical evolution of the health care system and its ongoing transformation. Designed for advanced students, the course provides an in-depth understanding of the economic forces and regulatory frameworks that have shaped the pharmaceutical landscape. The course consists of three modules: (1) The historical foundations of pharmaceutical regulation and financing, (2) the current economic and policy environment, exploring key drivers of pharmaceutical pricing, access, and innovation, and (3) forward-looking analysis, equipping students with the tools to predict the impact of proposed policy changes.

The Seminar in Dissemination and Implementation Science is intended for students enrolled in the Graduate Certificate Program in Implementation Science. This semester-long course can be taken for .5 or 1 credit hours and will require students to attend seminars or workshops in Dissemination and Implementation Science offered in-person (locally or at national conferences, etc.) or virtually. Students will be required to attend events (seminar or workshop), engage in the discussion/activities of that seminar/workshop as appropriate, and submit a structured reflection on the event to the course instructor within one week of the event. In collaboration with the Dissemination and Implementation Core of the Utah CTSI, a curated list of potential events that fulfill the requirement of the seminar will be made available to students. Credit hours and duration of the seminar determine the number of events a student needs to attend each month. For example, .5 credit hours requires one event per month for one semester (4 events), whereas 1 credit hour requires two events per month for one semester. The curriculum emphasizes the pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases of body fluids testing, including specimen collection, processing, assay performance, and result interpretation. Problem-solving, troubleshooting techniques, and quality assurance and improvement practices are incorporated to foster critical thinking. The course also includes instruction on safety processes/procedures required to work in a clinical laboratory and is designed to promote the student’s development as a healthcare professional.

Clinical Immunology is an introduction to basic immunology. The course reviews theoretical principles of immunology and provides an overview of using basic immunologic, serologic, and molecular technologies to diagnose disease. Hypersensitivity, autoimmunity, immunodeficiencies, tumor immunology, transplant medicine, serologic detection of viral and bacterial diseases, and immunization and vaccinology will be discussed in detail.

Discussion of leukemias, other hematologic malignancies, and special laboratory testing procedures will be provided.

Students work under the guidance of a faculty mentor to explore an in-depth topic in medical laboratory science and engage in honors research.

In the first section of the course, basic principles of research will be covered including how to identify research topics, evaluate the literature, construct and test a working hypothesis, analyze and interpret data, and report results. Basic research terminology and major formats of research designs will be discussed. In the second section, students will learn about basic principles of education including writing and evaluating learning objectives and examination items as well as teaching techniques especially those relevant to the medical laboratory, Topics related to accreditation, certification, and licensing in medical laboratory science will also be discussed.

Clinical experience in pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical testing of blood and other body fluids for their biochemical components (e.g. blood gases, hormones, vitamins, therapeutic drugs, trace elements, toxins) using modern analytical techniques (e.g., electrophoresis, immunochemistry, chromatography, spectroscopy, mass spectrometry).

This course is a clinical rotation designed to provide students with hands-on experience in diagnostic microbiology within an affiliated clinical laboratory. Students will gain experience in specimen processing, culture techniques, microscopy, identification of clinically significant bacteria, including anaerobes and mycobacteria; antimicrobial susceptibility testing, infection control practices, and quality assurance procedures. Modern and rapid identification techniques such as MALDI-TOF and molecular detection methodologies will also be covered. Through observation, practical exercises, and interactive discussions, students will strengthen their ability to think critically, perform troubleshooting, and interpret laboratory results. Professionalism, ethical conduct, adherence to regulatory standards, and biosafety are also integral components of the experience.

This course explores the biology, clinical significance, and diagnostic principles of fungi and parasites encountered in the clinical laboratory. Students learn and apply identification techniques using classical methods such as microscopic examination and culture, rapid assays such as lateral flow immunochromatographic tests and germ tube analysis, and advanced instrumentation such as matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization–time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS). Emphasis is placed on accurate interpretation of results and reporting to ensure correct organism identification.
The integration of the theory and practice of immunology in a clinical setting including immunologic assays used in the diagnosis of infectious disease, autoimmune disorders, and immune deficiencies.
Nucleic acid isolation, identification and amplification techniques used in disease diagnosis in the clinical laboratory.

This elective course provides students with an opportunity to build upon knowledge gained in previous MD LB courses. During the clinical rotation, students have the opportunity to learn from newborn screening professionals as they perform molecular and mass spectrometry testing for inborn errors of metabolism, hemoglobinopathies, and other inherited conditions. Students will learn how they can apply theory and skills gained in previous MD LB courses to the type of testing performed in newborn screening laboratories and explore newborn screening as a potential career path.

This elective course provides students with an opportunity to build upon knowledge gained in previous MD LB courses. During the clinical rotation, students have the opportunity to learn from medical laboratory professionals as they perform diagnostic testing in a rural clinical laboratory. Students will observe and assist medical laboratory professionals, whenever possible, in the day-to-day operations of a rural clinical laboratory. Tasks may include, but are not limited to: test performance, evaluating quality control, routine instrument maintenance, troubleshooting instrumentation, result review, and workflow management.

This elective course provides students with an opportunity to build upon knowledge gained in previous MD LB courses. During the clinical rotation, students have the opportunity to learn from forensic toxicology professionals as they perform medicolegal testing of biological specimens for driving under the influence (DUI), drug facilitated sexual assault (DFSA), and post-mortem investigations. Students will learn how they can apply theory and skills gained in previous MD LB courses to the type of testing performed in forensic toxicology laboratories and explore forensic toxicology as a potential career path.

This capstone course is designed to enhance students' clinical rotations by providing an opportunity for reflection on events, test results, ethical situations, troubleshooting problems, and other experiences that occur during rotations and professional practice. Throughout the course, students will work with a faculty mentor to explore a case study that incorporates two or more fields of study in laboratory medicine. Students will also participate in an interdisciplinary case study assignment with students from other health professions to foster teamwork, communication, and a deeper understanding of the roles and responsibilities of various healthcare providers. Students will also have the opportunity to evaluate their own professional behavior in the context of collaborative practice.

This capstone course enhances clinical rotations by providing structured reflection on events, test results, ethical issues, problem-solving, and other experiences that occur during practice in both Utah and international settings. Students participate in a global experience in international laboratory medicine through University of Utah-affiliated laboratories and an international community laboratory site, comparing practices across these environments. This course also emphasizes interdisciplinary learning through case studies that integrate multiple laboratory medicine disciplines and collaboration with peers from other health professions to foster teamwork, communication, and understanding of healthcare roles. Students assess their professional behavior within collaborative practice.

This 1-credit elective course is designed to stimulate the development of creative and critical thinking skills within the context of a specific research area (to be determined each year). Participants will learn and practice multiple techniques that can facilitate identification of potential areas for research and development of research questions. They also will learn and practice observational and curiosity-building skills. The specific research topics on which this course will be determined based on the interest of participating students.

The Rural & Underserved Utah Training Experience (RUUTE) program is excited about the rural research opportunities planned for medical students in the upcoming academic year. The Research & Innovation elective is an opportunity to explore the fundamentals of research and scientific communication and inspire future physicians and clinician-scientists to discover how patient care and diagnosis, prevention and treatment of disease can be largely influenced by biomedical research. Students will also participate in a Research Symposium once they return to campus to share their findings to the School of Medicine community. Upon completion of the elective, students will have developed a broad understanding of rural populations and their health-related issues, challenges, and determinants and the culture of rural and/or underserved communities.

This elective provides a strong foundation for students in educational scholarship, a foundation upon which they can build throughout their careers as they act on a commitment to continuous quality improvement of their professional practice as clinicians, teachers, mentors, etc. The course utilizes an individualized learning plan that balances individual reading and project work with synchronous and asynchronous on-line group collaborations requiring up to 10 hours per week.

The course would be a yearlong quality academy for students to learn QI principles and then practically apply those skills to a longitudinal QI project based out of the student led clinic. This course would include short lectures throughout the year on certain QI principles for the purpose of their project, with concepts being cemented through action and experiential learning as they will be conducting their own projects throughout the year. This will require development of critical thinking skills as students put together stakeholder teams and perform PDSA cycles.

This course focuses on foundational medical sciences. Each week has a predominant theme and integrates the learning of anatomy (embryonic, microscopic and gross, including cadaver dissection), basics of pathology, physiology, genetics, pharmacology, data analysis, metabolism and nutrition, etc. in a clinical context.

This course integrates foundational medical science topics covered in the Essentials 1.2 course with related material from the Doctoring 1.2 course. Areas of emphasis are the gastrointestinal and reproductive systems, along with associated principles of metabolism, nutrition and endocrinology, including underlying principles of anatomy, physiology, and disease processes, as well as clinical context.

This course will expose students to the day-to-day responsibilities and challenges of the medical profession. By shadowing physicians at a designated clinic(s) throughout the semester, students will gain in-depth knowledge of different specialties, medical environments, and providing exceptional care to patients.

This 1-credit course is designed for medical students who are interested in a broad overview of global health. Course topics include: Introduction to Global Health Principles; The Global Burden of Disease; Social & Environmental Determinants of Health; Human Rights, Economics & Development in Global Health; Injuries & Trauma: Case Studies in Global Health; Health Implications of Migration, Travel, War & Displacement; Malnutrition & Food Insecurity Across the Globe.

This course is designed for medical students who desire to meld the theoretical knowledge related to maternal-neonatal health obtained from on-line learning combined with the practical, hands-on skills acquired by completing structured Master Trainer workshops related to the care of the newborn and mother. Students will be required to complete two on-line learning certificates related to neonatal and maternal health in addition to two Master Trainer workshops, Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) or Essential Care for Every Baby (ECEB) or Essential Care of the Small Baby (ECSB) or Helping Mothers Survive (HMS).

This elective may be individualized to meet the expectations of the student, including clerkships in a hospital or clinic or research in a public health or clinical setting. Students will work closely with their designated local and on-site preceptors to ensure a meaningful and ethically-guided learning experience. The student will be expected to work 40 hours per week in the designated setting. Students can choose from one of our partner sites or set up their own. Independent site must be approved by the GHE office prior to registration.

It will be the responsibility of the student and the SOM preceptor to ensure that this is a valid learning experience in a setting that will not put the student at risk of too little or too much responsibility. The students will be expected to work 40 hours per week in the designated setting under the supervision of a qualified SOM and on-site preceptor. Significant health disparities in the United States are a growing concern. Developing a comprehensive understanding of tribal, rural, and underserved (TRU) population health and the inequities with which these communities contend, is vital for all physicians. This introductory course will explore the social determinants of health, and the complex intersectionality inherent in our system, including the challenges in caring for a wide spectrum of rural communities (i.e. tribal communities vs. ethnically diverse Hispanic centers vs, LDS enclave vs. racially-mixed communities of the African American South) and medically underserved urban communities. Though the geographic, demographic, and socioeconomic characteristics in the rural and urban underserved United States are remarkably diverse, medical practice in these communities (especially in rural and frontier communities) requires a broad skill set given 1) the wide range of medical conditions health care providers in resource-limited environments must manage, and 2) the local and regional leadership roles that these clinicians are often asked to serve, related to community-oriented health improvement interventions, administrative and educational leadership, and development and implementation of health policy. By participating in this course, and others in the Tribal, Rural, and Underserved Education (TRUE) Certificate, medical students will examine TRU population health through the lens of public health, social determinants of health, and health delivery systems, thus building a foundation of knowledge, attitudes and attributes essential in successfully responding to health inequities in TRU communities. This is a required course for MS1s interested in completing the TRUE Certificate. However, this course has no prerequisite requirements and can be completed by any medical student who desires to explore TRU health. Students taking this course will have the unique opportunity to develop a longitudinal relationship with a primary care clinical mentor. Students (OPTIONAL Opt-in opportunity for 0.5 credit) will be paired with a primary care physician (Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, OB-Gyn, or Pediatrics, depending on interest and mentor availability), allowing for a rich clinical mentor-mentee relationship to develop over the course of the semester. Students will spend a minimum of 4 clinical sessions during the semester, though, depending on time and mentor availability, more sessions can be scheduled.

Significant health disparities in the United States are a growing concern. To successfully address these challenges will require a multi-faceted approach across all aspects of the health care delivery system, and society more broadly. Developing a comprehensive understanding of tribal, rural, and underserved (TRU) population health and the inequities with which these communities contend, is vital for all physicians to understand, especially for those who intend to enter TRU primary care. This course, the second in a series for students interested in developing foundational knowledge in TRU health and who are working towards completing the TRUE Certificate, will explore tribal, rural, and underserved (TRU) health care systems, delivery, and resources, the knowledge required to address health challenges and disparities in TRU populations, and implement solutions to these intransigent problems. Though this course is required for the TRUE Certificate, it has no prerequisite requirements and can be completed by any medical student who desires to explore TRU health care systems, delivery, and resources. Students taking this course will have the unique opportunity to develop a longitudinal relationship with a primary care clinical mentor. Students (OPTIONAL Opt-in opportunity for 0.5 credit) will be paired with a primary care physician (Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, OB-Gyn, or Pediatrics, depending on interest and mentor availability), allowing for a rich clinical mentor-mentee relationship to develop over the course of the semester. Students will spend a minimum of 4 clinical sessions during the semester, though, depending on time and mentor availability, more sessions can be scheduled.

The Tribal Primary Care Clinical Preceptorship will expose medical students to the diverse knowledge, role and capabilities required of health care providers practicing in remote, resource limited tribal communities.  Students will have the opportunity to work with primary care and specialist preceptors in a variety of outpatient, inpatient, emergency, and surgical settings that serve Tribal communities.   Students will also be introduced to other elements of the health care delivery system, which support and complement the services provided by clinicians practicing in remote settings.

This course will provide a survey of the basic models that intl health systems follow - the Beveridge or single provider model, the National Health Insurance model, the Bismarckian model or non-governmental insurer model, & the out-of-pocket model - & use these peer comparisons to better understand the American healthcare system, which is a complex amalgam of these four models. The course will study international examples of each system (the UK, Canada, Taiwan, & Germany), including the underlying political & economic forces that led to their development, their evolution over time, & current functioning. We will turn to the U. S. in more depth, attempting to understand the logic of prev. & current reform efforts & pursuing guided research on topics of personal interest to each student.

The RUUTE Community Preceptorship elective will allow medical students to explore medical practice in rural communities across Utah, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming. Students will be exposed to the diverse training pathways that lend themselves to rural practice by having the opportunity to rotate with one or many preceptors including Family Medicine, Med-Peds, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, OB/GYN, Psychiatry, Neurology, Surgery and/or Emergency Medicine across the community. Other specialties will be considered on a case by case basis. Students will be exposed to a diverse range of healthcare delivery systems, observing how these systems serve clinicians, patients and communities as a whole. This course can be taken concurrently with RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE). Students must enroll in both courses individually.

Students will learn various strategies to examine health from a population level perspective. This course will provide a refresher on the basic principles of epidemiology & biostatistics. Students will gain hands-on experience by examining several public data repositories where population health level data can be accessed & analyzed. The course will have a focus on discussing social & environmental conditions which affect the health & wellbeing of populations. Students will also engage in methods for recognizing & addressing various biases in research, including personal biases.  Learning will include a blend of self-directed & active learning methods.

The RUUTE Community Engagement Experience (CEE) is an opportunity for medical students to gain hands-on clinical learning for a longer period of time than medical students typically get during their 1st and 2nd years of medical school. During this course, medical students will travel to a rural/underserved location in Utah, Idaho, Wyoming, or Montana to complete hands-on learning with providers of different specialties. Students will also participate in volunteer opportunities within the community. Additionally, they will be required to gather community specific data and complete community interviews to identify a pressing health concern in their community. Through the knowledge learned from these experiences, medical students will create and disseminate a community deliverable/intervention that addresses the public health concern they identified.

During this course, medical students will travel to a rural/underserved location in the Intermountain West to complete hands-on learning with providers of different specialties. As part of this 4-week rotation, students will meet their 2-credit hour requirement in health system science by gathering community specific data & completing community interviews to identify a pressing health concern in their community. Through the knowledge learned from these experiences, medical students will create & disseminate a community deliverable/intervention that addresses the public health concern they identified. At the completion of the experience, they will develop a poster presentation that reflects their community data & intervention that will be presented in the fall during a research symposium.

UUSOM students pursuing a Graduate Certificate in Rural and Underserved Medicine (GCRUM) must complete a Community-Oriented Health Improvement (COHI) Capstone Project during a 3rd or 4th year elective to earn the Graduate Certificate. This mentored 4-credit elective, along with the rural, underserved and community health prerequisite courses (MD ID 6550, 6555, 6660, and 6665), will provide the foundational principals and experiential support needed to successful complete this capstone. With assistance from the Course Directors, students will identify a mentor with knowledge and experience in community health collaboration and quality improvement efforts. Identifying a mentor can begin as early as MS1 – the sooner this process begins, the greater the opportunity to consider the many options available across the University and within the community. Faculty leads in rural and underserved medicine will assist students in identifying a COHI-project mentor, who may be a faculty member from any number of Schools or Colleges across UU (School of Medicine, School of Dentistry, College of Nursing, College of Pharmacy, College of Health, College of Social Work, College of Education), or a partner in community health outside UU (ie Utah Department of Health, Utah Department of Human Services, Utah Department of Workforce Services).

This course is intended to provide interested medical students with a way to get clinical elective credit by participating in student-led clinics. Students enrolled in the elective will further the service/learning work of the clinics in ways that go beyond their required involvement. Students will enhance their communication and patient interaction skills when working with a diverse patient population, gain deeper understanding of the cultural diversity and its impact on health care delivery as they coach more junior students, serve as a qualified interpreter*, fill vacancies in patient-care schedules, and/or complete other tasks as assigned by clinic leadership. Students will be able to tailor their participation according to their schedules and unmet needs of the clinics, including a 2 to 4-week block rotation or a longitudinal series of half-day sessions at times available during concurrent courses and spread over 1 to 2 semesters.

The Medical Students as Teachers elective prepares medical students to become effective teachers for their residency and beyond by participating in one of the UUSOM preclinical or clinical courses in an instructional role. Students will receive didactic instruction from educational experts on learning objectives, pedagogy, assessment, feedback, and evaluation. Students will apply knowledge and skills gained from didactics and reading to take part in structured and monitored teaching activities. The type of teaching project will be determined by a student's individual learning plan and area of interest (e.g., teaching at the bedside/in clinic, teaching in small group, teaching in large group, etc.). Students will receive guidance and feedback on their teaching project from a UUSOM faculty mentor.

The Students as Teachers Pathway I course will serve as the introductory course for first year medical students interested in participating in the Students as Teachers (SaT) Pathway. The course will help students determine whether the SaT pathway is the good fit for them and will provide a foundation in topics including: the role physicians play as educators for patients and the community, medical literacy, the unique role of residents as teachers, characteristics of effective feedback, and the variety of careers available in medical education.

The Students as Teachers Pathway 3 will serve as continuation for session content delivered during SaT Pathways 1&2. The course will build on teaching skills incorporated during the preceding pathway sessions, and will focus on more advanced topics in education including medical education research, presenting effective ‘chalk talks’, assessment and evaluation and role-modeling in education in the clinical setting.

The Students as Teachers Pathway 5 will serve as continuation for session content delivered during SaT Pathways 1-4. The course will build on teaching skills incorporated during the preceding pathway sessions, and will focus on more advanced topics in education as they present in the clinical setting while on clerkships.

The Students as Teachers Pathway 6 will serve as continuation for session content delivered during SaT Pathways 1-5. It will be a longitudinal course that will span the MS4 year, with 2 sessions in the fall and 2 in the spring taking place in the early evening to help accommodate clinical schedules. The course will build on teaching skills incorporated during the preceding pathway sessions, and will focus on more advanced topics in education and navigating a career in medical education, and will culminate in presentations of completed Capstone projects. During the course, participation in a structured teaching elective or the Getting Your Ed in the Game: Student Participation in the MedEdMorphosis Change Initiative elective is strongly encouraged. Based on the preferences of enrolled students, session will be live or via Zoom. Zoom sessions will be recorded for asynchronous availability.

All phase 3 students will complete 1 credit of near peer teaching and mentoring.  Students are expected to complete 1 credit (approximately 40 hours) of teaching and mentoring experiences.  They will be able to choose from a variety of offerings such as teaching assistant, mentoring of junior students in student led clinic or leading learning sessions during intersessions. This course will consist of experiential learning with application and reflection. In addition, students will complete knowledge modules specific to their experience and be expected to reflect on their experience at the close the course.

This course offers a unique opportunity for medical students who are new parents or primary caregivers to receive course credit for their valuable lived experiences that shape their personal and professional growth. Caring for a newborn or supporting a relative through significant health challenges brings its own demands; it also fosters resilience, empathy, and insight. The course is centered on self-directed learning, including curated readings on topics such as parental and caregiver mental health, lactation, and other aspects of caregiving. Students will also participate in weekly check-ins with a course director and submit weekly reflections based on readings and topics discussed during each meeting. The course is structured around current caregiving resources, research, self-reflection, and personal application. It will consist of independent learning, reflection, and four in-person, synchronous 1:1 meetings with a course director.

All students of the new MD program will participate in monthly Academic Half-Days and a Fall and Spring Intersession during Phase 3a.  Content will focus on knowledge, skills and attitudes required of all physicians, including professional identify formation, preparation for residency applications and core pillar content. Academic Half-Days will be held one afternoon each month.  The Fall and Spring Intersessions will be held during a 5-day interval between block rotations. Learning methods will include house and learning community activities, large and small group sessions, simulations and selective experiences. Of note, some monthly academic half-days may be conducted remotely.

Medical School Admissions Experience (MSAE) MD ID 7240 is an asynchronous (100% online) elective offered during the 4th year of medical school. This course will guide medical students to understand the theory and practice of admissions and to further develop leadership and organizational skills. Medical students can use this gained knowledge during the residency application process, as well as for future leadership positions. Such information and training will also be beneficial to preparing for and thriving in diverse organizations as a higher education leader within academic medicine.

Personalized Health Care is the tailoring of medical treatment to the individual characteristics of each patient. This course will review the fundamental elements of Personalized Health Care, discuss relevant case studies of preventative and therapeutic applications of Personalized Health Care, and explore future developments. Students will also have the opportunity to devise ways in which Personalized Health Care can be advanced locally, nationally, and globally.

This course will introduce students to the health issues affecting transgender patients. Through lectures, clinical exposure, and community opportunities, the students will explore discrimination issues, social and legal challenges, primary care and transgender specific care including surgery, and specific challenges related to the pediatric and adolescent transgender population. This will be structured as a continuity course, which will be spread over a full academic year in order to maximize clinical exposure in this multidisciplinary field.

Brain and Behavior 3.0 is a MD Program course that all students will complete during Phase 3. The course is 4-weeks in length and integrates clinical and foundational science and skills required of all physicians. With regards to the clinical experience, students will complete two weeks of clinical service on a consultative behavioral health team and two weeks on a consultative neurology team. Students will integrate behavioral health and neurologic foundational science into their clinical experiences. Their study will be rigorous and build on concepts learned prior to Phase 3.

A Longitudinal Integrated Clerkship is a model of clinical education in which students participate in the comprehensive care of patients over time, engage in continuity of relationships with preceptors, patients, health system & the surrounding community, while meeting core clinical competencies across multiple disciplines simultaneously. The specialties included in this introductory clinical experience include Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Neurology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, and Surgery. Settings for clinical experiences will be predominately outpatient with intermittent inpatient immersions. The Urban Underserved Longitudinal Integrated Clerkship will focus on medical care in underserved communities in the greater Salt Lake area.

The course aims to use the value equation as a backbone for introducing important health system science topics to students. We will build upon our experience in directing the Value Driven Healthcare pathway to provide foundational knowledge with the following objectives: Understand the value equation in healthcare (interplay of quality, service, cost), introduce students to healthcare economics principles, describe the impact of payment methods on the provision of healthcare, and understand the basics of quality improvement methodology.
The course includes asynchronous and synchronous methods to introduce students to CDS tools, implementation, design and future efforts.
